utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please announce the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is case -- against -- [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by our intern, Lisa Hartog, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Could the Defence also introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. I am Edina Residovic, defending Mr. Hadzihasanovic, and we have our case assistant with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. For Mr. Kubura, we have Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today on the 26th of January, 2005, the Chamber would like to welcome all those present, those from the Prosecution and those from the Defence, the accused, as well as all the other persons in the courtroom and around the courtroom and who are assisting us to work. Today we will continue with the cross-examination. And I do not wish to waste any more time. I would like to hand the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination, unless the Defence wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we promised yesterday, document DH0232 [as interpreted], which did not have the second page translated, we have provided the translation in its entirety and we would like to present that, because perhaps our colleagues from the Prosecution would need to use that in the course of their examination. So I would like to submit the translation of this document to the Chamber and to our colleagues in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is document is 0832, DH.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There was a mistake in the transcript. We are talking about 0832 and not 0323. The Chamber doesn't have a translation of this document. Yes, we now have everything that we need. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to pick up where we left off yesterday, which was with the issue of foreigners in the primary school in Mehurici. You told us, sir, that - and this is at lines 18 and 19 on page 81 yesterday - "I didn't exactly pay attention to the date when they left." And I'm wondering, sir, if you can give us an approximate time period when the foreigners left the Mehurici primary school based on the information that was made available to you.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I had in early December, or in late November, so that was that period, in early December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, or based on any information that you may have received, did any of the foreigners remain at any point in the school or in any location within the primary school in Mehurici into 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, absolutely. This was not something that I took any interest in. I didn't have time to deal with that, so I don't know exactly whether any of them stayed or where they went exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now to ask you a couple of follow-on questions - excuse me - with respect to the issue of the armed Mujahedin or the armed foreigners. You told us yesterday, sir, that the first time you saw them was on the road. You -- you told us that they shared -- that they were travelling on a road that you often travelled on yourself and that was the first time you saw armed Mujahedin. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only road. There was no other road. Everyone used it, not only myself and the Mujahedin. The Croatian population, the Bosniak population, they all used that road, because it was the only road that you could use to move. So you could meet anyone. Anyone could meet anyone else on that road. It wasn't a special road for the commander or members of the 306th or for the Mujahedin, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that, sir, but my question was simply: You told us yesterday that the first time you ever saw the Mujahedin was on a time you were travelling on the road and you saw them on the same road.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In the Biljani Valley was the first time I met them and saw them. As we were passing each other in the cars, I noticed them. I turned around and I noticed them, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time period when you first saw the armed Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the end of the year, perhaps in the month of January, in early January. In that period I saw them. But it's hard to remember because it was such a long time ago. It's hard to remember the details. I saw a lot of soldiers of all sorts, from the HOS, from the HVO, the army, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "January," that would be January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what I thought, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it then, sir, that at no point in late 1992 or in the autumn of 1992, when you were with the Territorial Defence in Travnik, did you ever see armed foreigners in Travnik, in the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I never saw an armed foreigner while I was in Travnik. Absolutely not. I saw foreigners passing by, passing through. There were foreigners there. I did see them. There were UNPROFOR soldiers; they were foreigners who were there on their missions. As far as Arabs, those foreigners, if that's who you mean, I did see them in Travnik around the town in civilian clothing, in their traditional clothes, yes. But I did not see any of them in uniform with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So then, sir, at no point in 1992, just so we're clear, at no point in 1992 did you see armed Mujahedin in the area of the Medresa in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to this road that you've told us about in the Biljani Valley, where you first saw the armed Mujahedin, on how many occasions did you see armed Mujahedin travelling on that road?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I travelled in the morning and in the afternoon or early evening, I would encounter them rarely. Perhaps they did pass by. But when I used that road, it was night. It was dark. It was winter. So it would start to get dark around 4.00, between 1600 and 1700 hours. I would stay in the command to work until 2200 hours because I was dealing with the formation of the brigade, so I couldn't really notice it at night. But on a couple of occasions when I was travelling during the day, that's when I was able to see them and that's when I noticed them. But in other -- other times, other occasions, I didn't have the opportunity to encounter them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on this road that you've told us about in the Biljani Valley, did the HVO maintain any checkpoints along that road during the time period that you're discussing?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were several checkpoints. Not one but several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time during this time period, did any units of the ABiH maintain checkpoints along this road?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that same road, the army did not have any checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did units of the ABiH, including the 306th Mountain Brigade, experience difficulties getting through these HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have difficulties. At least my assistants, my officers, informed me when they passed that they did have certain problems. I personally also had problems because they knew that I was a commander, and I would go to the HVO brigade commander, Frankopan, and we would cooperate, be resolving issues, and I warned him several times that I had problems, that his soldiers were stopping me frequently and asking to check me, to do controls. And I asked him at least not to do that as far as I was concerned. However, it was no good. Every day when I passed, I would be stopped, checked. I didn't go through anything in particular; however, my officers were mistreated to a certain degree, disarmed. Their technical equipment was seized. I mentioned that, computers and so on. This was something that happened practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any of these meetings or discussions that you had with the commander of the HVO brigade, Frankopan, were complaints about the Mujahedin raised with you?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, nobody insisted much on that or initiated that question, as far as the Frankopan Brigade was concerned. But as time went on - we're talking now about April, May - then certain questions began to be asked about these foreigners, about their stay. So perhaps in March, April, and May, that's when these -- the question of these foreigners became topical, when certain conflicts began in Central Bosnia, Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, Vitez, that's when they were the subject of discussion or the topic of interest, those foreigners, at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about access through the HVO checkpoints on the road in the Biljani Valley by the Mujahedin. Do you have any information or knowledge as to how the Mujahedin were treated at any of these checkpoints on this road?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I really don't know. Perhaps you could ask the HVO how they dealt with them, how they released them. But there was nobody who would convey such information to me, not the HVO or they themselves. I cannot really tell you what they did or what problems those people who had checkpoints had with those people, but they probably didn't have any major problems. If we see where these foreigners came from, how did they come. This is a hypothetical question. They had to have come from somewhere. How did they get into this territory, and so on and so forth, without any problems. To arrive from a certain territory to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina without any problems, while a member of the army, the B and H army, could not go anywhere. Why? I really never went in-depth into that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it then, sir, from your answer that you have no idea or no information about where these foreign Mujahedin who were in Central Bosnia came from?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the Travnik municipality, where I saw them in civilian clothing, I saw them with vehicles with Zagreb license plates, in jeeps. They were civilians who were there, and I was asking myself how come they were there. How did they get here from Zagreb? It was a bit unclear. The whole situation was unclear. But this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were with the Territorial Defence in Travnik or later with the 306th Mountain Brigade, did you receive any intelligence or security briefings concerning the armed Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally did not receive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you at any --

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time when you were with the Travnik Territorial Defence or commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, did you direct any security or intelligence officers within your command to obtain information on these foreign Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, as commander of the 306th Brigade, as I said yesterday, besides providing certain -- well, actually, they were not the topic of interest of the 306th Brigade. They were not in its jurisdiction or of any interest to it. Primarily our aggressor were the Serb forces, and we would collect intelligence data about them or information. However, like I said yesterday, when the foreigners started to create problems in the functioning of the brigade, we would report to our superior command about that. We received certain instructions to collect data about them. And I said I did go to see if I could find anything out, who they are, exactly what they were doing, what their objectives were, and so on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In the last period, after I left, I don't know whether they were of interest, as far as intelligence data was concerned or whether any directives were given. I really don't know. Once I left the brigade, nobody requested any information about that from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Other than when you were directed from a superior command, did you on any occasion order your 306th Mountain Brigade, security service, or assistant commander for intelligence to gather any intelligence information on the armed foreigners within the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that you received from the organs, it was not possible to get any information. These were people who were not professionals. The information that I did have available, I did pass it on to the people in documentation. Whatever I found out about them, I informed the superior command. I didn't keep anything to myself. There was no need for that because had it been my unit, I would have had to resolve that. However, I passed it on to the superior command as the responsible officer, as the responsible superior, who had to pass on any information, facts, the situation. I had to acquaint my commander with that. Otherwise, how was he to make decisions? I didn't conceal anything. Whatever I knew, I sent it up -- along. Whatever I didn't know, I just didn't know. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in passing this information up the chain of command, did you expect your commander to resolve the problem?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know what the jurisdiction or the competencies of my corps commander were, and that's logical. I was expecting a certain amount of help. How were we supposed to resolve these problems? Probably my superior also requested help from somebody else. I don't know that. I requested it because I believed that there was nobody else who was going to help me except my superior commander. And when I received returned information, then that was something that I implemented. How successful that was or could that have been even more successful is something that could be re-examined. But I did say what kind of personnel I had available to me. They were untrained officers. And you yourself know how much an intelligence officer had to be trained, how much training they needed. I know that in the old army, in the JNA, such cadres were given particular attention and special training. These people never had anything to do with that kind of job before in their lives and during the war they were finding out exactly what that work was, and so on. So there are methods; however, we did not have the option to apply all of those methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us approximately how many armed foreigners were in the area of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I really wanted to know, but I was never able to find that out. In order to know somebody well, you would need to find out everything about them, what their weapons were, what type of weapons they had. I didn't know anything about them. I knew that they were there, that they had a camp, that it was secure, that they didn't allow access to anyone. And I knew that myself. I didn't know of a way to get to that information, how to find out that data. Also, believe me, I had so many other problems that I didn't know what I could do there. They were not the only problem that I had. Had that been the case, it would have been much easier. I had the HVO in the immediate vicinity. I also had the HOS, which is an even more extreme section of the HVO. So all of them would come there and create certain problems and so on and so forth. I also had some renegade members of some units and brigades and so on. Also, in my area - you must understand this - in the areas that were under the control of the army, the organs of the civilian authorities were also functioning. It was not a total military administration. The MUP had their own people there, the civilian protection, and there were other organs there other than the army's. These people were not members of the army. How was I supposed to treat them, in what way? Perhaps other people had jurisdiction over those bodies. That's something that I don't know. But I know that I was responsible for my brigade, for my men. I was the commander. So everything that prevented me from functioning as a commander and as a brigade, any kind of problems -- if they were inside the brigade, I would resolve them. If not, and if such a problem happened to be interfering with my work as a brigade, I would inform my superior commander. And this is how it's usually done in all the other countries in the world. This is the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the problem of the Mujahedin ever rise to the level where it threatened your ability to command the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to that extent. They didn't attack us. They didn't disarm us. They didn't physically abuse us. They didn't interfere in our communications. I told you what their basic problems were yesterday. The -- their attempt was to win over some more people into their ranks by propaganda. I didn't have any problems that they were blocking the barracks or that they had formed a front line in relation to us. They simply closed themselves up within a certain area and functioned with that area, the way they were. However, when they came to the village and were trying to promote their cause amongst the people in the village or when they were telling people not to go to the lines but to sit in their camp where they had certain activities - I don't know what they were doing - and they offered these people money for that. On the other hand, I was not able to give them money or food or anything, but I was making them go to the front line. These are -- were my problems, and I consulted with the command about how to resolve these problems. This affected my work. I had soldiers, believe me, who had 11 children. I had one soldier who had 11 children. He couldn't do anything because he was mobilised into my brigade. So can you imagine how he was supposed to survive? During the war, I had one child, and I hardly survived, and I was the commander of the brigade. So I responsibly state that my child ate jam for two months, the jam that my wife made. What about my soldiers though? It was difficult -- it's difficult perhaps from this time -- distance to understand what the circumstances were at that time. They were not disarming me. They were not preventing me from moving around and communicating. They were not interfering with me in any way. And I had no jurisdiction in this matter. These were my problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did the presence of the 306th -- or did the presence of the Mujahedin, the armed foreigner, have a negative impact on morale or good order and discipline within the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, we're confusing things here. Their actions, what they did, the things that I told you about, did have negative effects, and this is why I reported about this, because the people who were going to them had everything provided for them and I was not able to do that for them. If any soldier left, he would weaken my unit. He would weaken our combat ability. And this is something that I informed the superior command about. Whatever directly affected my unit, that bothered me and that's something that I would report about. If they hadn't done that, they would not be something that I would be interested at all. I wouldn't have any problems with them. I had a mission received from my commander. That was my line of defence. I was supposed to implement that and that is my task. As for everything else, how the territory is being controlled, how the civilians functioned, along the depth, that is something that I absolutely had no interest in and it was not in my jurisdiction. If, however, I did encounter some problems, I had to say, "I have such and such problems. I cannot function properly." Then I don't know whether perhaps the military authorities were instructing the civilian authorities to do something about this or giving them directions. That's something I don't know. I was at an altitude of 1600 metres. I didn't have any problems up there. They didn't go up there. They weren't there. I was up there with my soldiers and I was guarding the entire Travnik municipality from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, other than the camp run by the Mujahedin in Poljanice, were you aware of any other areas within the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility where there was a concentration of armed Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the brigade commander, I didn't know anything about that. I was only aware of Poljanice, first of the school and then of Poljanice. Later on, I don't know whether there was any -- a particular camp or a place where they gathered and stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how far was the Poljanice camp from the school where the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade had its command post?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I am not a native of that area, I don't hail from there, it's very difficult for me to say, and I was there only once. There was no need for me to take that road. It's a blind alley and it doesn't lead anywhere. It's very difficult to say, but I don't think it was more than 2 kilometres from one place to another. I never measured the distance and it's very difficult for me to say how far it was as I sit here. You can look at the map. And if you want me, I can look at the map and give you the -- a more precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me move on to a -- to a slightly different topic. During the time period that you were the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, were there any foreigners in the 306th Mountain Brigade or any of its subordinate units, including the battalions and within the battalions, the companies and platoons?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility while I was the brigade commander from November up to mid-August, there were no foreign members of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you told us that during this period from November up until mid-August, when you were the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, that your brigade maintained positions along a front line that extended approximately 25 kilometres. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time during the period that you were the commander did any other units of the 3rd Corps operate with your forces along that 25-kilometre front line?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question. Are you referring to my area of responsibility, the one that was assigned to me, or did you refer to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me rephrase the question so that we're clear. The 306th Mountain Brigade had an assigned geographic area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the nine -- approximately nine-month period that you were the commander of that brigade, on how many occasions did other units of the 3rd Corps operate within the zone or area of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this happened on the 8th or on the 9th, to be more precise. Members of the HVO in concert with the Serb forces abandoned the lines that they had been holding. On my left flank, there had been members of the HVO up to then. On the 8th and on the 9th, they abandoned those lines. They informed the Serb forces that they had abandoned their lines, and they gave them the green light to start moving towards Travnik. Luckily enough we received intelligence on that and we reacted very quickly. A unit of the 17th Krajina Brigade was sent there to take those lines in order to close the front line. The Serb forces had already been almost a kilometre up to the line, and luckily enough we were managed -- we managed to stop them. Because if we hadn't, they would have achieved their goal, and that was to take Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- the transcript at least in English says this happened on the "8th or on the 9th, to be more precise." Can you give us the month and year you were referring to when you say "on the 8th or 9th"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the month?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, other than this occasion on the 8th/9th of June, 1993, did any other units of the 3rd Corps operate within the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the case. If this had happened on any front line, I would have known that. Maybe you're talking about cooperation. We cooperated with -- with the 314th Brigade, but it was not in my zone. They were on our right flank. We linked up with them. We were in combat together, but not within my zone. I had my zone of responsibility; they had theirs. But we acted in concert. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive any information or intelligence about the armed Mujahedin engaging in combat at any point in time during the period Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you were the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received certain information from my intelligence officer. According to that intelligence, some armed Mujahedin were reconnoitering some axis facing the HVO and they undertook some activities on their own, independently. We didn't know what they did. They were there, and the HVO opened fire on them. We lodged a protest because we didn't know what this was about. And then members of the HVO informed us what had happened, because this was not on our line of defence. This was the line of defence that was manned by the HVO, especially facing Mehurici and Suhi Dol. They had firing positions. They had trenches. They had minefields. And while we were up there thinking how we were going to stop the Serbs, they were making their lines around the Bosniak villages. And the HVO had certain problems, and in the month of April and in the month of May the issue of Mujahedin was raised. And I believe that the HVO did have certain problems with them. I myself did not have any such problems. And when I say that, I mean attacks, sabotage attacks. At that time, I had problems with the HVO, not with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware at any point in time -- let me ask you this: This incident that you've told us about, can you recall approximately what month and year these events took place?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this happened before the events in Miletici. This happened some seven days before, around the 20th of April. This is when this happened. These events preceded the developments in Maline [as interpreted], the incident in Maline. This is according to the intelligence that we had. I don't know whether there were any other incidents, because nobody informed us. We did not have that information, or at least I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I suppose this is a mistake in the transcript. The witness mentioned Miletici and then in the transcript we read that this happened before the events in Maline.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Miletici, not in Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware at any point in time of reports or information about the Mujahedin engaging Serbian forces on or around Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I know what was happening on my defence line. How was I supposed to know what was happening on somebody else's defence line? The commander who was in charge there did not send information to me. He sent information to his superior officer. As far as my zone of responsibility is concerned, I am not aware of any such thing happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the time period that you were the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, did your unit maintain a war diary or a war log?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But during the period when the command was fragmented, this was very difficult because the command did not act as a command. Everybody was somewhere else, and wherever they were, they did keep some notes. I'm talking about the period when the command was broken up, between the 20th of May, 1993 onwards. The command was not reunited before the 18th or 19th of June, and it is then when it started working as a proper command. That's when we had daily briefings, an exchange of information among the members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, where was the 306th Mountain Brigade war diary kept?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was with the operations officer. The chief of staff was the most responsible person, and he was in charge of the war diary. He made sure that it was kept, and he made sure that I was informed and kept abreast of the most important information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently, sir, did you personally review the war diary of -- of the brigade that you commanded?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I had an opportunity to do so, and especially during the period starting with the 25th. I was not in a position to review the diary at all from the 25th May 1993 up to July or August. There were times when I didn't sleep for seven nights in a row. The situation was so difficult that I did not see my family for a month and a half. My wife and my child were in Travnik, but I did not have a possibility to go and see them, let alone the war diary. My family was more important than anything, but I couldn't see them. Because there was fierce combat taking place, and it was hard to know who was shooting from where. There were daily attempts on the part of the HVO to regain the lines that they had lost, and they would launch a counterattack after a counterattack. I was dealing with so many problems. I had a 25-kilometre-long line up there and I received a new 25-kilometre-long line down there on my own. My brigade was poorly equipped. My soldiers had 10 bullets each. One had to be a magician to deal with that. We were lucky that the HVO was not very good at reconnoitering. If they had been, they could have done us a lot of harm. All sorts of things were happening during the war. Unfortunately, we would have been so much better off if there was no war, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that a small number of exhibits be shown to the witness. We distributed these to the Defence yesterday. And if the usher could perhaps assist us with this. We unfortunately don't have them tabbed. But the first one I'd like the witness to be shown is P679. The documents are in numerical order with the English on top, followed by the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a quick look at this document. Sir, is this a document that you drafted and submitted to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me personally. This was done by my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't sign it at the time, but I'm familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, sir, to paragraph C, which is on the first page of the document, and I have a few questions for you about that. If you could please -- if you could please read out, sir, the first two sentences -- or three sentences of that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Frequent cases of all forms of crime in our zone of responsibility recently have damaged the combat readiness of units." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And for that very reason, the security situation is visibly impaired." Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please read the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Muslim units which are stationed in our zone of responsibility contribute to this significantly. They are financed by people from Arab countries, so they have purchased plenty of MTS [phoen]. The perpetrators have been discovered through efficient activities by the military security service and the military police and criminal reports have been submitted against them, which has greatly contributed to the fact that crime in our zone of responsibility has been reduced to a minimum." Q. Sir, can you tell us what the reference to "Muslim units which are stationed in our zone of responsibility" refers to?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: People describe these forces with different words. Somebody called them "Mujahedin." Somebody called them "Muslim forces." Somebody called them "Arabs." But they had in mind the same people. We did not have a standard name for these people, and everybody referred to them as they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So this reference, are you saying, sir, could be to the Mujahedin; it could be to the Muslimanske Snage, the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Q. Can you tell us what it means when it says "the perpetrators have been discovered through the efficient activity by the military security service and military police"? A. They were 25 discovered, and I saw those criminal reports. Members of my brigade had sold 1 them some of our equipment. This was probably one of their goals, to disarm 2 the brigade and to weaken its combat readiness. The security officer was in 3 charge of investigating any possible crimes. If he was aware of something 4 like that happening, he would take steps…or prevent, then file a criminal 5 report and inform me that a criminal report had been filed.After that I had 6 no authority. It was up to the judicial organs to prove or establish what 7 happened. I know that four criminal reports were issued against four people; 8 one of them was Jasarevic. One of those four was selling equipment to people 9 who were not members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So your military security office had the authority to arrest the foreigners who were buying this equipment from members of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If any of my men were selling arms to anybody, to a civilian, for example -- I didn't have anything to do with the civilian, but I could take my man to task for having done that. All this -- all the weapons that my men had, they had bought with their own money. We did not have any weapons that we could provide them with. People seized weapons or bought them. That's the weapons that they had. I, as the brigade commander, never provided anybody with a weapon, because I didn't have any. I did not provide any of my soldiers with a single bullet. They bought them themselves. And still we tried to prevent them from selling those weapons. Some did because they didn't -- they had to survive. But if we had allowed one to sell their weapons, the flood gate would have been opened. That's why we fought that. My security officer had the -- the authority to fight against that and informed me of the things he did in order to prevent those things from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, let me see if I understand what you've told us. Some of your soldiers had to buy their own weapons because there weren't enough weapons for the army to issue them weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some? All of them. All of them. All those who had weapons had to buy them themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And some of these soldiers were then selling these weapons to the Mujahedin or to members of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or anybody else. There were such attempts to sell weapons to either Mujahedins or civilians. And whenever we learnt of that, we tried to prevent such transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why would it be unlawful for a soldier to sell a weapon to a third party if he himself had purchased the weapon and it wasn't issued to him by the army?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It goes without saying that this is the case. But the situation was such: We were facing extermination, and I was aware that my soldiers had their own private property which was not supposed to be violated. However, we had to organise ourselves. We had to help each other in order to survive. If we had waited to receive weapons from anybody, we would have never gotten it. You know that there was an embargo, and we would have faced extermination worse than Ahmici, worse than Srebrenica. I'm sure that you're aware what was happening to the Bosnian people in Bosnia. If we had not taken timely measures and if we had not kept those weapons for us, regardless of the fact that it was private, then we wouldn't have survived. The situation is different now. I was a soldier before this war, during that war, and after the war. And whatever I learnt before the war was completely different during the war. The situation was what it was. During the time of peace, I'm sure that a soldier who was prevented from selling his own property would sue his commander or the army, but at that time we had to make do with what we had. If we would not organise ourselves, if we did not do everything possible to organise ourselves, I wouldn't be sitting here today, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the Mujahedin doing with the weapons that they were buying from your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask them. I don't know. I was the commander of the 306th Brigade. Ask me what my men did with the weapons in the 306th Brigade. You have to ask them. You have to see why they needed the weapons in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd ask that the witness now look at P660.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you take a quick look at this document, and is this -- does this document bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you, sir, if you could focus your attention on the final paragraph of this document, under heading number 3, that indicates "unusual incidents and relations with the HVO." And I'd ask you, if you could, quickly read that part to yourself.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it out loud or just for myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself, the final paragraph under number 3.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, the incident that's described in this paragraph, did that happen within the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not my zone of responsibility. My zone of responsibility and my line of defence was shared by three brigades, so it was hard to tell whose zone of responsibility it was. There was the Frankopan Brigade, the 306th Brigade, and one part of the 314th Brigade. And this incident happened on the road that the HVO constructed. This was a new road that was constructed in 1992. I have told you already that from March onwards the Mujahedin did carry out certain activities independently, and maybe this is what caused it. This was not my zone of responsibility. Do you know what "zone of responsibility" means? You have a certain width, a certain depth, and so on and so forth. We had a line of defence facing the Serbian forces. In the depth of that area, I did not have any responsibility. There were three MUP stations. There were civilian bodies. There was an HVO brigade. And this particular area was more leaning onto the area where the HVO brigade was. This is where we had to pass my bodies, my organs, my police. They had to pass on that road, and we noticed that. We reported it. And then an investigating judge came and took over from us. It was our duty to report to the competent body that a dead body was seen on the road. A judge was sent to that place, and I don't know how the whole thing ended. It was not up to me to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you know -- how did you know, sir, that this incident caused disgust among some members of the 7th Muslim Brigade? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, if you were following me, that some parts were -- went renegade, who represented themselves as being members of the 7th. But in later contacts, the commander of the 7th separated himself from those individuals, and in the village they were protesting against those cases. We really thought that they were members of the 7th. And that's how my assistant received information from those villages, that those people had come from the 7th Brigade. And of course he informed the superior brigade to see who are these people, is there a 7th Brigade. I didn't know where that was located, what were its tasks, was it there, and so on. However, he relied on information from certain villages. He had positions in villages. You know how security organs operate. They had positions in the villages amongst the soldiers and so on. I don't know what the source was, but this is the information that he got. He checked it with the commander, and yesterday you saw in the exhibits that we warned the commander of the 7th, that there were certain individuals who had a negative effect on conduct, security, and so on. However, he replied that they were having certain problems, that they had renegade groups, and so on. And I told you that from the Bila Valley soldiers were being acquired for the 314th, 306th, 307th, 312th, and the 17th Krajina Brigade. But it's very difficult for me to check. I cannot stop these people and ask for their identification. That would be very difficult to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, the identity of any of these so-called renegade members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for a commander. Believe me, I didn't even know the names of my own soldiers. I was able to find out the names of my immediate associates, people that I cooperated with from the brigade commands, the company, and the unit commands, and so on, where I was a bit further removed, because the duty of the commander of a platoon or of a company is to know the names of all of his soldiers. My task was different. My main task was to form a unit, prepare it, train it, and also take up and maintain the lines. I was constantly being warned by my commander that this was what I had to do. That was my main mission. Everything else was secondary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you direct the military police assets of the 306th Mountain Brigade to arrest any of these renegade 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, subordination, the lines of subordination are well known. I'm sorry, but if I need to repeat again the authorities of the brigade: There is the corps police, the operative group of the brigades, and the brigade police. The authority of the brigade police was only for members of the 306th, so I could not use my police to arrest any other member from any other brigade, because each brigade had its own police force and they took care of their own members. I could not issue orders for a member of some other brigade to be arrested. I don't know at that moment whether such and such a person was from the 7th or not. If my soldier from the 306th did not come or if they violated some rule or something, I could arrest them. The other information I would pass on to the superior command, and then they could instruct the brigade where a particular soldier was from, if further steps were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you didn't know which brigade the soldier was a member of, how could you categorically rule out the possibility of arresting such a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, according to that, I could have arrested members of the HVO who would commit or cause certain incidents. They were also in a uniform. Why? Well, we happened to be allies at that time. Another thing: My commander, my security organ is from that area. All the police officers, the soldiers, were from that place. They knew each other very well, where who was from and so on. I was in a different situation. I know every man in my own village, the village where I was born, where he comes from, and so on. But people just knew that it wasn't our member or it would be written down that it wasn't our member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a look, please, at the next document in the collection, which is P661. Can you tell us what this document is about? Again, specifically with reference to the first paragraph, where it talks about certain members of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult. I see the document, but it's a little bit hard to read. Let me just read it, and then I can comment on it. It's very difficult to read. This passage is talking exactly about what we were commenting on a little bit earlier. We had information that they were members of the 7th, and this is what we put down. However, in further activities -- and we received a response to this from the 7th Muslim Brigade. They had distanced themselves from such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no transcript. [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, sir, if you could please turn to the next document, P662, which is a daily operations report dated 8 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think it might be fair for all the parties if I make this point at the outset. This is the first time this document has been shown to a witness, and there is a translation problem which I wish to bring to the attention of Your Honours. It may need to be sent to the -- the Translation Unit, but it appears on the face of the document to be quite an obvious error. And that is, Your Honour, at the bottom of the first page of the English translation, it reads that "There have been some cases of members of the 7th Muslim Mujahedin Brigade being mistreated." That is an incorrect translation of the original in Bosnian. There is a whole word missing, Your Honour, and that word is a very important one; it's -- it's "and." The correct translation should read that "There have been some cases of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin being mistreated." If Your Honours look at the Bosnian original over the page, it's the word "odnosno," that is, in the original Bosnian but has not been translated into the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I did want to point that out immediately so that if there are questions asked, the confusion doesn't arise, because in the English version it would appear that the 7th Brigade is called a Mujahedin Brigade, but in the original that's not the case; it just reads "The 7th Muslim Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That was precisely why this document is being shown to this witness as a starting point. I appreciate my learned colleague's comments. I would ask that this document be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of the interpreters in the booth. I fully expect we will need to send this document to CLSS for further translation. I'm going to ask the witness to read out that paragraph. I believe it would be of assistance to our friendly colleagues in the booths to have that document placed on the ELMO, and I will then ask the witness to read out that entire paragraph and then we can go through the usual procedure of sending it off to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I fully agree with that proposed procedure. If I could mention though that the rest of the paragraph has another "odnosno" mentioned in it. That's further down. That's two lines down from the section that we say is incorrect. And that has been properly translated as "The HVO and their command." It goes on from there. So it would appear, just from a plain reading of the paragraph, that when that word is properly translated as "and," the English translation is entirely incorrect. I do appreciate my learned friend's suggestion that it can be corrected now through it being read by the -- the witness and -- and translated. And of course the witness can comment on the document because it appears that -- that it's his document. Thank you, Your Honours, for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir if you could take a look at the document that's to your right on the ELMO. You may also be able to observe it on the screen. Let me ask you, first of all, sir, if this is a document that you signed and submitted both to the 3rd Corps operations centre and the OG Zapad command in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't draft the document, but I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you if you could, under paragraph 2, read out loud please the third paragraph under section 2, the one beginning "With regard to the security situation." If you could read that entire paragraph out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With regard to the security situation, it is satisfactory. Relations with the HVO are currently favourable, except that there have been some cases -- there have been some cases of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, meaning the Mujahedin, being mistreated at checkpoints controlled by the HVO. Because of this, we would ask the relevant command to send an appeal to the HVO units, meaning their commands, to" -- well, it's a little bit difficult to see -- "their commands to" -- it's not easy to see -- "to stop these excesses because they could lead to undesirable consequences."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, can you tell us, when you just read out the document, you said "some cases of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, meaning the Mujahedin." What do you mean by that or what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you are familiar with the way in which reports are written. All the command organs participate according to their segments, so the intelligence sector deals with the aggressor. That's done by the security organ. Then own forces is done by the operative chief of staff. The security situation is done also by the security staff. So the assistant commander for security received information through his channels probably that certain members of the 7th, who are perhaps coming for a rest from the brigade from Travnik to their houses -- I said there were members of the 7th from my territory, people who were in that brigade. And probably when they came for a rest at home, they experienced these incidents and probably this incident showed that foreigners who were passing through were receiving special treatment. Like I said, from March -- from February, March, the intensity of the checks of foreigners and all the other members became more intense and more strict. Probably he had certain information, this assistant commander. Probably they were thinking about the 7th Muslim Brigade, those who were coming. It was in Zenica, and it was in Travnik from -- so when they were coming from Zenica to my area, they had to cross the Ovnak road where members of the HVO had a checkpoint ever since they were in that territory. So this is my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try the question again: What is the reference to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Mujahedin" in this paragraph? What -- what is that a reference to in this paragraph, in this document that you submitted to your higher command?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably those persons who I mentioned earlier that I encountered passing through the checkpoints in their vehicles. That's probably thinking of them, who were using the road going towards Travnik or Zenica. I don't know where they were going. They were going, and probably my security organ had certain information, whether this was from members of the HVO or from somebody else. You know, that security organs had positions on other sides, in different areas. So he probably had access to certain information. I don't know. You would need to ask him about that. But a part of what he knew has been written down in this report or included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try this, Colonel, one more time and then perhaps we'll take the break. My question is: The document that you signed submitted to your superior commands says "Members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, meaning the Mujahedin." That's what you've told us it said when you read the document. That's my question. What is the connection between the Mujahedin and the 7th as stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't want to -- I don't want to stop the witness from answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to be very precise because I believe that this question is not clear enough. The Prosecution puts to the witness the following and wants the witness to say that members of the 7th Brigade or, in other words, the Mujahedin. That's at least what I derived from the French translation and from what I read in English. The word in English is "meaning," and it is translated into French, and this is what I receive. The Defence, what -- what do you have to say about this question? I would like to hear you before I give the floor to Mr. Mundis. Mr. Dixon, can you clarify things for the Judge here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- but if the witness could perhaps be taken out of the courtroom before we discuss this any further, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Firstly, if I can say there's no objection to the witness answering the question about what he means by "Mujahedin" in the document. And it is a important question for him to clarify. My objection relates to the way in which the document has been translated. The witness has not said when he was reading out the document that 7th Brigade means Mujahedin. That's what the translation booth said, and that's what I've got in English, and in French it's come across in a slightly different way. "In other words" is the way it's come across in French. Our objection is that the word that has been left out of the English translation, "odnosno," they referred to earlier on, simply means "and." This is confirmed by another translation of that word, "odnosno," just a few lines down where in the original it says "The HVO odnosno," and then it goes on, and that is translated as "HVO units and their commands" And our submission is simply that it should be translated consistently throughout the document. It's being translated as "and" a few lines down and it should just be translated in exactly the same way a few lines up. It should read: "The 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin." We say that is absolutely the correct translation of this document, and that's what should be put to the witness. And then his answer, whatever that might be, is something separate to -- to be recorded. But we must have an independent, verified meaning for the -- the document in English and in French. And in our submission, it doesn't mean "meaning the Mujahedin," or "in other words the Mujahedin." It doesn't mean either of those. It simply means "and." It's referring to two separate entities, in our submission. Perhaps we could use the break to see if that could be clarified with the translation booths and then put the question to the witness thereafter. In our submission, it would have to be clarified by the Translation Unit in any event. So it will still have to be sent to the Translation Unit. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon has just said that the word "odnosno" means "and." And this is what he already said. The interpreters, however, have translated this word differently. They didn't say "and." They translated this word as "meaning," or "in other words." So we have a problem which has to be solved. Before we take the break, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, and they have to take into account the words of the Defence and they have to take into account the possibility that the word "odnosno" means "and," rather than "in other words" or "meaning," which would imply that the members of the 7th Brigade were also the Mujahedin. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position has been quite clear and quite consistent with respect to interpretation or translations of documents. We have no objection with that being done. I will note, however, that in the course of the witness reading this out, the interpretation booths translated the word "odnosno" meaning "meaning," in both contexts. That was pointed out by Mr. Dixon, and that's reflected in lines 12 through 20 of page 31. They -- the interpretation booths here translated that term consistently, notwithstanding the defect, if there is one - and I think it's probable that there is - in the written translation. I simply point that out in the event that we can't get this resolved very quickly over the next break in terms of wishing to ask this witness the very question that I proposed putting to him, which -- which drew the initial comments from my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the other team may help us with that. They are specialists for B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this may be interesting from the linguistic point of view, but you will be able to interpret the significance of this document once you hear the witness, because the word "odnosno" can be interpreted as "meaning" or "in other words," but it can also serve as a conjunction when you enumerate things. In our language, it depends on what the author of the text wanted to say. The word "odnosno" can be translated differently in other languages. I personally believe - and I agree with my colleague Dixon - that in this particular case this word means "and," i.e., it serves to enumerate things. It's up to the translators to resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification. We are going to take the break. We will resume around ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the interpretation is concerned, the Judges have discussed the matter during the break. There are a few things that have to be mentioned. There is a dictionary, B/C/S and B/C/S into English. We have consulted Benson, which was printed in the United States at the University of Pennsylvania. And in this dictionary, it says that this word means "in other words." So according to Benson, it means "in other words," or "more exactly" or "to be more precise." According to the interpretation service, this word can also mean "and," but it depends on the author of the document. The author can use this word as meaning "and." The interpretation service has given us a written explanation of things, and this is it. However, this does not prevent the Prosecution from interpreting the document which was written by somebody, not by the witness himself. The witness signed it, but maybe the witness can give us his interpretation of the document. We are going to bring the witness into the courtroom, please. The time that we have just spent in discussing this matter will not be counted as the time used by the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if we could again turn to P662, this paragraph that we were discussing prior to the break. And I would like you to tell us the phrase that you read out: "The 7th Muslim Brigade, meaning or in other words the Mujahedin." Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here these two things are separate. This is not one thing. There are members of the 7th, on the one hand, and then a comma, and then the others, who are the Mujahedin. In this context, this is not one thing. As far as I know the rules of our language, the comma here means that the 7th Muslim is one thing and the Mujahedin is another thing. This is my interpretation and this is according to the grammar of our language and this is also the reflection of the reality. Are you -- I don't know why you are confused. Are you saying that the two things here are the same? This is not true. This does not stem from the document, and this does not stem from the reality of the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what information you had about Mujahedin being mistreated as checkpoints controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any, because I wasn't interested in them. It was my assistant for security who decided to inform the command about certain instances of ill-treatment at checkpoints. What did this mean for my unit for their combat readiness? Nothing. These were not my members. There was ill-treatment at the checkpoints. And this information was sent to the commander indicating that the situation might get worse. Because there was already tension in the air, and this meant that we as a brigade might face problems in the future and I would be responsible for that. I was responsible for that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm simply asking you a question. You told us that in the context of this document, the way it was drafted, the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin are not the same thing. You've just told us that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, this sentence then says: "Relations with the HVO are currently favourable except that there have been some cases of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin being mistreated at checkpoints controlled by HVO units." And my question to you is, sir: What information did you have about Mujahedin being mistreated at HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you. My assistant for intelligence and security received certain information, I don't know who from. I was not interested in either the checkpoints or the Mujahedin. I was not interested in the 7th Muslim Brigade or the HVO. However, this information might have had some repercussions on the territory where my brigade was, and these incidents might have compounded the situation. And it was within this context that this was mentioned. This information was sent to the superior command so that they could react. I as a commander was duty-bound to incorporate any information that any of my assistants might have had into our report. My assistant commander was under my command, but he also was in a different chain of command. He was subordinated to his counterpart in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of reaction did you expect the 3rd Corps commander to take with respect to mistreatment of Mujahedin by members of the HVO at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't expect anything. I don't know what the word "the authorities of the commander of the 3rd Corps" -- I just provided him with information. I don't know what his authorities were and what measures he was supposed to take, what measures he took for that matter. You have to ask him. I expected him to help me with my unit, and he didn't help me. I expected him to arm my unit and to help me with that. He didn't. As to -- as regards this matter, what he was going to do, I didn't know and it was not something I was interested in. However, we had to provide him with this information because this might have had repercussions on our situation, and that's why we did it. What he did after that, I don't know. You have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to document P663, which is the following document. It's a relatively long -- it's a three-page document, sir. I'd ask you, first of all, if that's your signature at the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute to look at the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a quick look at this document. I will tell you, however, that I'm primarily interested in asking you questions starting on page 2, the very last paragraph on page 2, and parts of the top of page 3 and then the proposal section. Can you look, please, sir, at the last paragraph on page 2 in the original, and it begins "Soldiers of other units." Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you read, please, the first two sentences of that paragraph out loud for us.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A particular security problem in our zone of responsibility are members of other units which have become renegades and are not under the control of their respective commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Read the next sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to read on? "They are primarily members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and we do not fully know the status of the Mujahedin. They and members of the 314th Motorised Brigade have committed arbitrary acts which further aggravate the already tense situation with the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us a little bit more or can you elaborate upon what you were communicating to the 3rd Corps and the OG Zapad commanders by way of this document.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to say that we have already discussed all of those issues. It is true that there are some people who are not under control. It is true that we are not clear on the status of the Mujahedin and this is beyond dispute. We have also mentioned members of the 314th who committed acts which were not in keeping with standards and norms. However, this is all beyond my authority. I was not responsible for the 314th. I was not responsible for the 7th. I was not responsible for the Mujahedin. I informed my command that the things that are happening on the ground are aggravating the situation, which was true at the time. And this caused certain problems and this resulted in further tensions between the HVO and the 306th Brigade. I was aware of the situation in my brigade, and if the things got out of hand, then how was I supposed to control my members?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you now to look on page 3, under the heading "Proposals," or "We propose." I would like you to read out the fifth proposal listed on this document. If you could read that out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To resolve the status of the Mujahedin and members of the 17th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici." Should I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine, sir. Let me ask you this: What -- this reference in this document to the 17th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici," can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be a typo. There was never a 17th. There was a -- the 17th Krajina Brigade. I believe that this was a human error. It is a typo to my mind. It was not spotted when the document was being sent. I believe that the reference was made to members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, rather than the 17th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there --

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. I'm sorry. The second proposal refers to the 17th Mountain Brigade, but the fifth proposal refers to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I believe that the person who typed the document made a -- a typing error. So these are two different proposals. One of them refers to the 17th Brigade, and the -- the other one refers to the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, this document is describing the period 15 April through five May 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about this 7th Muslim Brigade or members of the 7th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici? Can you tell us what that's all about?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again: In my zone of responsibility, there were soldiers who belonged to the 7th Muslim Brigade of the 314th and so on and -- so on and so forth. They were not only from one village. They were from a number of villages. And I don't know how many members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were from the Bila Valley. You should ask their commander that. Nobody had to provide me with that information. The truth is that they were from the Bila Valley. Already in May the Bila Valley was completely encircled and nobody could leave the Bila Valley. It is quite probable that people from that area were resting and they could not leave the Bila Valley. They could not join their unit. They were probably there staying with their families in their houses because they couldn't report either to Zenica or to Travnik. Also, there were some rogue soldiers, some renegade soldiers of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, sir, if you at any point in time became aware of the identity of any of these rogue or renegade soldiers of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I wasn't interested in that. They were not my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't belong to me. The person they belonged to or the unit they belonged to had to take interest in them, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, why under this fifth proposal on this document, P663, you proposal resolving the status of the Mujahedin and members of the 7th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici in the same proposal. Why are those two items lumped together in this proposal on this document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a compound report covering a certain period. This report unites all the previous information. All the problems that I listed were present in my zone, and if those problems had been solved, I would have no problems. A lot of things would have been better if these problems had been solved, and that's why my proposal was for these problems to be looked at and solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, that you've listed a number of proposals that you would like to be resolved. My specific question is: Why you list the Mujahedin and members of the 7th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici in the same proposal, in the same phrase, rather than considering them as separate problems.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a technical issue. There's no essence to this. This is a technical issue. These could have been two different proposals. One has nothing whatsoever to do with the other. It is just a matter of technical approach, how this proposal was worded. The person who drafted this report did it this way. He could have done it differently. Maybe this proposal could have been number 1, because it was more important than anything else. I'm sure that the person who received this report and read it knew exactly what this was all about. We're talking about technicalities of writing a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, sir, you signed this document the way it was drafted and presented to you. Did it occur to you to say, "Wait a second. These are two different problems," or in your mind were the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade members quartered in Mehurici one in the same?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we are talking at cross-purposes here. We're talking about grammar, about linguistic problems. You can name ten different problems within one single sentence without putting these ten things in the same context. These are two different problems, two different things. It was just a technical issue. This is the way the person who drafted the report worded it, and it's a technicality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just turn for a second to another paragraph in this document so that we don't have to come back to it later. Earlier, sir, I asked you to look at the last paragraph on page 2 in the original language. I'd like you now to look at the first paragraph on page 3. And in the English version, this is the first full paragraph on page 3. And I'd like to ask you some questions about what's being reported in that paragraph. And again, it starts "On this occasion." Can you please read that paragraph out loud to us, please. And perhaps if you'd put it on the machine to the right, the interpreters in the booth will be able to see precisely what's written in the document. Do you see the paragraph I'm referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
