utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could please read that out to us.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On this occasion, without giving a description of the event, I would like to mention the attack on Gornji Miletici and the looting in Dolac Purici, the expulsion of Serbian families from Mehurici, the daily instances of fire being opened on HVO members and retreating." This is out of the context. You have to read the previous paragraph first because the previous paragraph will probably tell you why this was so. If you will allow are me to read the previous paragraph, this would put things in perspective. Can I look at the previous paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely that. These problems that I have just read about are within that context. Shall I read the entire thing? That would give us the whole context. The paragraph that I have just read out has been taken out of the context. You have to read the last paragraph on page 2, and you will see that this paragraph is compatible with the following paragraph, which is on page 3. This is just a continuation of the same thought that starts on the previous page. You can read it. I can read it. Anybody can read it and you will see that the reference is made to that thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's be -- in order to save time here, sir, because you've already read that paragraph out loud to us and because everyone in the courtroom has a copy of the document in front of us, let me just ask you some further questions, then. This paragraph talking about the attack on Gornji Miletici, what was that all about? When was it and what units or -- or forces were involved in the attack on Gornji Miletici? During this time period covered by this report.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It referred to that because in the prior report, those from the brigade involved immediately in the events in Miletici processed completely that event in Miletici. In order not to repeat everything in this report, this time they had said that they did not want to repeat things that had already been reported. So it refers to events on the 25th of April, 1993 the Mujahedin attacked the village of Gornji Miletici, killed five civilians, and arrested the others. However, being persuaded by members of the 1st Battalion and my assistant for security, they persuaded them to release these people also because of the fact that one of their fathers was arrested. They assumed that members of the army accommodated those people and kept them alive. I got a report how it happened. There was a joint HVO and army commission which confirmed the report and the description of the events in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: You've just told us that this paragraph with the reference to Miletici relates to the preceding paragraph, the paragraph coming before. Is that what you told us a few moments ago in relation to the context?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, a part of the excerpt refers to the report, especially to a report and also to these problems here which are being mentioned in this passage, especially the problems with the Mujahedin. But there is a previous report about who did what in Miletici, and then they say it here in order not to repeat a description of what happened in Miletici and then these problems which are in the context of what is happening here. This is a continuity of reporting and probably the person who received the report knows what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To what extent does the information in the preceding paragraph, which mentions the 7th Muslim Brigade, the Mujahedin, members of the 314th Motorised Brigade, how does that relate to the paragraph describing the attack on Gornji Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, these problem, these Mujahedin who had evaded control, specifically there, that they had units which were out of control of their superior command are primarily members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the status of the Mujahedin is not fully known. So the Mujahedin were evading control, so they in this context did this in Miletici. So without repeating the description of the events that had taken place, because prior reports spoke about the incident in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you now to move on to P704. Perhaps the usher can assist with finding that document. Did you in fact sign this document, sir? Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- what this document is all about, sir? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What is this reference to "Staff belonging to the 7th Muslim Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have previously stated that from my part of the territory for the needs of the 7th Muslim Brigade a number of conscripts were mobilised. I told you that in May the situation was that the valley was entirely blockaded. Most of the members were from the village of Kljaci from the 7th Muslim Brigade and they happened to be resting at home on their regular leave and they were unable. Now, we're talking about the regular parts, the regular parts. And they reported to my commander that they wanted to place themselves at the disposal in order to defend their villages where they were living, where they had their families, because they were not able to go to their units, so that they could be engaged for guard duty and the immediate security of the village of Kljaci and they requested me to allow them to do this and of course I permitted them to become part of the village forces because they were from the village and that they could organise the defence, just like any patriot from the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at the top right-hand portion of this document there is a security classification. And I'm wondering if you can tell us based on your career as a military man who or what authorities indicated this document was top secret and very confidential. Do you see that on the top of this document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army, we had degrees for each document from the superior command, what types of documents were to be given which degree of confidentiality, and that depended from document to document. This is part of command and control. Most of the documents are strictly confidential, internal requests, requisition forms. Logistics documents could be such but did not have to be so necessarily. It depended on what kind of a document it was and then it was given the adequate degree of confidentiality. Sometimes I want didn't have to do anything with the contents of the document, whether it was given a certain level of secrecy and confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, where in the hierarchy, if you will, of classification of documents top secret, very confidential fits into the scheme of things.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first are documents which are confidential, internally confidential -- strictly confidential, and state secret. These are the classifications for confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about -- this document, at least in the English, is translated as "Top secret, very confidential," and I'm wondering how that fits into the scheme.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What would you like me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what -- what the classification stamp of this document is? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states "Strictly confidential." There's nothing in dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you now, or perhaps with the assistance of the usher, if you could turn to P481. Sir, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just read it first? I have never seen this document before. And if I may comment, this document is illegal. Even if I had received it, it would have meant nothing to me. Correspondence of relations and subordinations in accordance with that, no one is obliged to act upon or take this document into account. It means nothing to me as commander of the brigade. It could be an internal matter for somebody, but it means nothing to me. Another unit, especially a unit of lower rank, or the same unit, the commander of the brigade cannot resubordinate somebody. I cannot resubordinate a part of my own brigade. And it is out of the question for somebody of lower rank to resubordinate somebody to me. This is something that could be only done by the corps commander. Had an order come from the corps commander, then I would be duty-bound to comply. But this is something that I'm seeing for the first time. The relationships are quite well known. It is very clear who has authority over whom and how that is carried out and respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on any occasion in August of 1993 did you meet with any of the UNPROFOR BritBat liaison officers in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. There were I don't know how many such meetings and when. If there was a meeting, that was scheduled by a British officer. I attended all the international meetings scheduled by the international forces. I don't know what this is all about. I don't recall whether I was there or not, but if you have any questions in relation to that, perhaps I can -- I can try to remember. Perhaps you can help me to recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- the very first document that's in the collection that you have, P355 - and the second page of the bundle would actually be the version in your language - is an internal UNPROFOR BritBat daily situation report. Now, sir, I wouldn't have expected you to have ever seen this document, but in this document the Travnik liaison officer reports a conversation that he had with you on the 7th of August, 1993. And I'm specifically interested in what he reported concerning this conversation as reflected in paragraph 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not go into any comment on this. This is not the proper context. I perhaps only warned or provided information, which was my duty to do, to provide the organs -- the international organs, that they could expect problems there so that they can be prepared. I was not trying to tell them to go and that they -- that if they went, they would have problems. I told them that if they went there, they might have problems. I was not able to protect them. I didn't have any control over that. I just warned them. But this comment, I have no idea which context he -- he drew this conclusion on. I acquainted the commander and the international factors that these people were there and that they could create problems. This was well-meaning information to these people, nothing other than that. I don't know how that officer understood that information at that particular time. That is something that I leave to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, my -- I guess my question is: Did you tell -- do you recall telling the liaison officer in Travnik on the 7th of August, 1993 that there were Mujahedin based in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that meeting. I am saying it again. But the problem of the Mujahedin did -- the Mujahedin was something that was discussed at a number of meetings. The officers would try to go through. They would be stopped. Then they would come to me asking to be able to allow to pass through Mehurici. That's something that they didn't write down, but they did write down this. I don't remember the context based on which they wrote down something like this. There were problems at a number of meetings. They had their own problems. They were unable to carry out patrol duties even though they had UN insignia and markings. I repeated several times that I did not have any authority there, that it was not in my competence, and that I was not able to help them there. I said that the Mujahedin were not under my competences and that there was nothing that I could do there. As far as the 306th was concerned, I said there was no -- no problem from at all. They could go anywhere and I was the one in that case who could guarantee them access and passage and the -- the ability to fulfil their mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall telling any of the BritBat personnel that a BH army commander should accompany them if they wished to move through that village? Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that they had to go to a command that was superior in relation to mine. They had to go to a higher command than mine; that would be either the operational group or the corps, that they had to try to cooperate with them. I would have resolved that myself had I had the proper competence in that matter, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you now, sir, to turn to the following document, P418. And as -- as the usher is assisting us with that, sir, yesterday in response to some questions from my learned friends from the Defence, you spoke about your commander ordering you to come up with three scenarios. This is on page 36, lines 2 through 9, and you described these three scenarios: One, an attack by the Serb forces; the second, an attack by the HVO; and the third, an attack from both sides. I'm wondering, sir if this document that you have before you - and I understand there's a blank plan page in the middle of this three-page document in your language - is this the document you were referring to yesterday when you talked about your commander ordering you to come up with a plan with respect to three scenarios?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, I direct your attention to paragraph 3.2, "Variant in case of attack by the HVO." I'm wondering if you can tell us why in the 306th Mountain Brigade plan you envisioned using part of the forces of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're coming back to this. This is a proposal. This is not a final request. The corps command requested a proposal from us. When they received the proposal, then they would draft the order that we were to comply with. This was our thinking and what we thought would be the best way to act. However, I said when we were working out all these options - this is from May - there were members of the 7th who were unable to reach their units and I asked for an order so that the commander could regulate that, that they could be part of the composition, but the commander never did that, and this plan was actually never implemented. It was asked for by the commander. I don't know why. He probably wanted to see if the units were ready and how he could issue the orders. But we never received a confirmation of what we sent out and we never received a returned order. This is just our thinking about how we could do something like this, what would be a good way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the combat activities that occurred on the 8th and 9th of June, 1993, were those undertaken as part of some kind of a plan? Was there a plan behind the combat activities of 8/9 June of 1993 in the 306th area in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no plan. And I repeat: The attacks on Bosniak villages of Ricica, Radojcici, Bandol, Bukovica which resulted in the 17 dead was not something that was ordered by me. I just asked for assistance from those officers who were in Mehurici. That was my operations officer, my assistant for logistics. I asked them to find any -- any way to help these people who were at risk. In those villages, there were members of the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of the 306th Brigade. And this was done spontaneously. And whatever was done did not resemble in the least the plan. It was done spontaneously. The officers who were there decided on the shortest possible way to help those villages that had come under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask with the assistance of the usher that the witness be shown DK22, which he looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps -- perhaps I'm not following what you've just said, but if you look at this document, which is from your brigade to the 3rd Corps, the very last sentence indicates that everything is going "according to the plan." And I'm wondering if you can just explain what -- what that means.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not draft this document. I saw it subsequently, after the events. At my request for assistance to be provided to these villages, I assumed that one part of my command -- I wasn't there. I just assumed. They drafted something. There must have been some sort of agreement as to how this would be done because they were leading people, not cattle. I suppose that they decided what to do and at the command post they were aware of some plan. And this plan has nothing to do with this order. Don't link one with the other. It was a hastily made plan which was drafted because of the situation. Otherwise, we would have been held heavily responsible if we hadn't done anything. So this was done in a haste, and it was some sort of a plan, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the period on the 11th of May, 1993, when you went to the camp in Poljanice. And for your benefit, sir, it might be -- if the -- again, with the usher's assistance, document 1007 in the Defence binder, which perhaps I can give you the tab number. It's actually the very last document in the entire binder, the very last document, which has been marked by the Defence 1007. Now, sir, this document, which is a report to the 3rd Corps military security body from the military security commander in your brigade, Mr. Asim Delalic, does this document accurately reflect --

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. He was not commander. He was assistant commander. There's a huge difference between commander and assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I -- I appreciate that correction, sir. The assistant -- his title was assistant commander for security in the 306th Mountain Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander for security in the 306th Brigade. That is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document that Mr. Delalic submitted to the 3rd Corps security body, does it accurately reflect the information that was obtained during the meeting you had in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report, the assistant commander was not duty-bound to keep me abreast of all the reports. He had his own link with his counterpart in the 3rd Corps. When I was in Poljanice, I -- I heard some things and I told him what to write about that. He, however, had some other information that he incorporated. As I already said yesterday, this is just one of the things that he knew. The assistant commander had other information that he incorporated into the report that he sent through his own chain of command to his counterpart in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and I -- I appreciate you informing us of that. My question though was: Does this document accurately reflect what happened in Poljanice when you went there on the 11th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: One part of this report reflects that. There are some other parts of the report that I was not familiar with. Some names are mentioned. And, for example, Alija Izetbegovic is mentioned, and Ramo Dervis, Sljivo Malik. I've never heard of these people before. I don't know who these people are. We were informed that they had received approval from the Main Staff of the BiH army that they would establish the 8th Muslim Brigade and that this brigade would be subordinated to the General Staff. This is what we discussed in Poljanice. The rest of the report was up to him, and it was how to -- up to him to incorporate into this report whatever he wanted without informing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No commander is aware of -- of what the assistant commander for security does or what measures he takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall or were you ever informed of the name of the Emir that you obtained information from in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I was never interested in that name in my capacity as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, towards the bottom of that document -- in fact, it's the last paragraph of this document -- it seems to imply that if the 8th Muslim Brigade would have been formed, the 306th Brigade would be disintegrated. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see that -- do you see that phrase there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did -- did Mr. Delalic discuss that issue with you and the possibility that the creation of the 8th Muslim Brigade might cause your brigade to disintegrate?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. These are probably his estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what these estimates are based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever come to a similar conclusion personally? In other words, did you ever think to yourself: If an 8th Muslim Brigade was created by these people in Poljanice, the 306th Mountain Brigade would disintegrate or would be threatened perhaps because many of its soldiers would have gone to this new brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not engage in speculations. We were a military. There was a command which issued an order for the establishment of the 306th Brigade. The same command could have ordered the disintegration of the 306th Brigade. It could have given it a different name. It could have done whatever. I did not engage in speculation. I had my obligations and I did not have other concerns. It was my commander who maybe was thinking about possible further moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you look now, please, at the preceding document, that is, number 0923, which is in the tab immediately -- again, this is Defence document or -- 0923. Sir, prior to coming to The Hague a week ago, a few days ago, et cetera, did you ever see this document before?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I am not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's not surprising, since this is a document that was an HVO document and delivered to Commander Blaskic personally.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot give you any comment because I'm not familiar with their correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you -- what you -- what you expect from me. What is your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's precisely my point, sir, is that you in the course of the war in April 1993 did not, as a matter of routine, read HVO documents addressed to Colonel Blaskic. That was not something that was a routine in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, this description in here, which the Defence asked you about yesterday, concerning events in Miletici, can you verify for us that this account, as set forth in this document, was not something that you were necessarily familiar with on the 26th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I was the commander of the 306th Brigade. I had my assistants, my organs. I had my superior command and my subordinate commands. The reports sent to me by subordinate commands are the ones I read. I read those reports and I received orders from my superior -- superiors. My superior was Mr. Dzemal Merdan, who was there together with others and he was involved in -- in investigations. If he had something to tell me, I'm sure that he would have. He would have either asked me to change something or to take some actions in my capacity as -- as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever receive any order or any request to prepare for undertaking any kind of combat operations against the Mujahedin from any of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You were never tasked with preparing for such action or gathering intelligence against them for purposes of undertaking combat action against them?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have changed your question now. Your first word was "attack." The second word you used was "gathering." Attack is one thing and we did not have such orders. However, we did receive orders for our intelligence organs to be activated in order to gather intelligence, because the commander believed that this was necessary and he ordered his assistant for security and this person in turn ordered my assistant to gather intelligence and to send that information to the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you briefed by your assistant commander for security at any point in time about the intelligence-gathering with respect to the Mujahedin within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and he was not duty-bound to inform me. His duty was to inform me about my problems and anything that had to do with the 306th Brigade. And as for intelligence gathered during his operative work, he's duty-bound to send that information to his counterpart, the assistant commander for security in the 3rd Corps. He was not duty-bound to inform me of any intelligence gathered during his operative work. The only case when he was duty-bound to inform me about such things was when the information was pertinent to the 306th Brigade. He sent his intelligence information to his counterpart, and I don't know where else they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a couple of questions about the events that occurred in Maline around the 8th of June, 1993. Can you tell us about the steps that you took as the 306th Mountain Brigade commander to investigate allegations concerning the deaths of Bosnian Croats that occurred in Maline Bikosi on the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already testified, I learnt about that on the 12th June 1993. My assistant informed me that this had happened and that the investigation was underway. As soon as I received that information, I issued an order to my assistant to send a report to the superior command informing them that this had happened and that the investigation was underway. I issued an order to my assistant to engage the police and the assistant commander from the 1st Battalion and to investigate. They did investigate. They briefed me. And since the investigation showed that members of the 306th had not taken place in that event, I was of the opinion that this was where my work stopped. I only asked them to inform the superior command that this had happened and that it was the Mujahedin that had done that. I believe that my authorities stopped there, that I did not have any other authorities with respect to that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now some follow-on questions, sir, in order to clarify what you've just told us. Do you recall approximately what time on the 12th of June, 1993 you were informed of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really recall it. It was during the day. I don't know what time we had the meeting. I really cannot remember. That was a long time ago. It was sometime during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you can tell us, if you recall, where you were when you were told this information and, again, the person who informed you about this.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying it again. I was in the village of Krpeljici and I was informed about -- informed about it by Delalic Asim, the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Delalic? It's now appeared in the transcript. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you then ordered Mr. Delalic to carry out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately when he informed me that there was a report, or to send the report and to start the investigation immediately. I didn't go into the methods that they would do. I was involved with the combat operations, so I was concentrating on my tasks. I tasked him with investigating it and informing me about the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you became aware of this initial information on the 12th, did Mr. Delalic inform you that the Mujahedin were responsible?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his assumption. There were indications about that. It was his assumption. He wasn't sure, but there were indications. Because I ordered that an instruction -- that an investigation be carried out. I was the one who asked him to investigate it, to find out exactly who did what. And he did the investigation, said that it was done by the Mujahedin and that they had taken a number of those civilians. And -- and I ordered them to report about that. They assumed in the investigation that no member of the 306th had taken part in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was the first time, to your recollection, that your superior command, the 3rd Corps, was informed that the Mujahedin were responsible?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information arrived on the 12th. It was sent to the 3rd Corps -- that there were indications. And then after some 15 days or so - because this was done by the security organ, not by the command and control - the investigation was conducted, and after that at a -- on or about the 27th of June there was this definite information, which I received, and I ordered him to pass that on to the higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the first time the higher command, the 3rd Corps, was informed about the involvement of the Mujahedin was about the 27th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one report on the 8th and then there was another report, if you understand me. There was one -- first, there were indications that this happened. An investigation was ordered. It was conducted. And then the results of the investigation were told to me, I as the commander. And then I instructed my assistant also to send written information to the corps command, to the assistant for security. That was also given -- that was what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time Mr. Delalic completed his investigation, other than providing you with the results, did he give you a briefing or explain to you the steps he had taken to conduct the investigation, such as his methodology, whom he may have spoken to, what he did, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't like that. I am not duty-bound to monitor him. I am not interested in how he will get his information. I am only interested as commander in the final information, because it's out of the question that I wouldn't trust my assistant. His superior could have checked on him and then he could suggest to me that perhaps he was not the competent person to do that and then a substitution could be suggested to the control and command and that another person be appointed to that post. Even I, as commander, could not replace this assistant, because it was something that was proposed by the administration for security of the General Staff. He is helping me, and he's there for my needs when I asked him to do something. But he also had other duties in relation to his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall if at any point in his investigation Mr. Delalic questioned you or asked you any questions about what units of the 306th Mountain Brigade may have been involved in any combat activities in the area in and around Maline? Did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with me. Again, that day, when it happened I was in Krpeljici. I wasn't even informed about it. I was woken up by shooting. I didn't know who was attacking whom. I wasn't able to command the units at that point in time. There was a team at Mehurici which was commanding those units. There was nothing that they were going to ask me, because I didn't know anything, up until that moment when he informed me what happened and I instructed him to carry out an investigation. He couldn't have asked me anything because I didn't know what had happened. I didn't know. I was isolated and surrounded, so I didn't know what was happening in the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me ask you about what you were told. Can you -- can you just briefly tell us what you were told happened in Maline Bikosi on the 8th of June, 1993 with respect to these Bosnian Croats. What happened? What do you remember being told happened?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember everything definitely. The only way would be if I had recorded the conversation. The most important to me from that investigation was whether members of the 306th took part in it or not, because I know what would then happen. I would need to take certain steps. So that was my focus, to find out that when he informed me that it was not done by them but by Mujahedin, I was no longer interested. The only thing I was interested in was whether somebody from the 306th was there, when they were taken away, and if any of them had participated in that. That was the main thing. They were -- there were witnesses there, police officers from the 306th, and who provided them with certain statements. So it wasn't interesting all that much to me afterwards, anything else. What I was most interested in was whether any of my members participated in that. But it's absolutely impossible for me to recall exactly how the conversation went. I cannot remember all of those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have just a few more questions, I believe, and -- and that will complete the cross, if I can continue for just a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, now, you also had information towards the end of April 1993 that the Mujahedin had committed crimes in Miletici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, once -- and did you know or have any suspicions or any knowledge or any information that the Mujahedin who had committed the crimes in Miletici had come from the camp in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't have information about that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But I believe, sir, you told us earlier that at least within the area of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade, which you commanded, you were not aware of any other areas where there were concentrations of Mujahedin, armed Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But there's nothing in that. I know about the camp in Poljanice. Whether it was them or not; perhaps it was; perhaps it wasn't. According to what the population from there said and the committees that went there, it seemed that the Mujahedin had done that. But where they were from, from this place or that place, that is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following the event in Miletici, did you issue any orders to the 1st Battalion commander or any of the other units within your brigade to avoid the Mujahedin camp near Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue any orders in that context, neither to avoid or not to go there. I don't know why I would issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me give you two suggested reasons why you might have issued such an order and see what -- what response you have. In the first instance, sir, if we -- if you had suspicions or any information that the Mujahedin had committed violent crime, they might pose a threat to your soldiers? And number two, because you've already told us that the Mujahedin in that camp occasionally offered money to your soldiers as a way of enticing them to join them. Did you ever consider saying in effect that the area around the Poljanice camp is off limits to 306th Mountain Brigade soldiers or the area extending, a perimeter extending 200 metres around that camp is off limits to 306th Mountain Brigade soldiers? Did you ever consider that for either of those reasons, that the Mujahedin might have been dangerous or the Mujahedin might have posed some kind of financial incentive or other incentives for your soldiers to go near that camp?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I would like to say: My soldiers, when they were on leave, they were at home in civilian clothing. I didn't have contact with them. I couldn't monitor them. I could do that only with those soldiers who happened to be on the lines of defence. What kind of a security measure could I have if they were at home? This wasn't a barracks, not a unit. My line was up there. Down there the people walked around like any other regular citizens. I'm thinking of members of the 306th. It wasn't a barracks where you could gather a unit together and tell them things. My combat tasks were in Vlasic. In the depth of the zone, I didn't have any duties, until the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, because I neglected to do so earlier: With respect to the events in Maline on the 8th of June, 1993, did the 1st Battalion -- did your 1st Battalion commander, the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, ever report to you about anything he may have discovered concerning the events in Maline?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would like to say that my assistant and the assistant battalion commander Zukanovic conducted the investigation together. The battalion commander had his own assistant, and these were the results. There was a joint investigation that was conducted by members of the 306th command and the 1st Battalion, and I've already told you what the results of the investigation are and I can repeat that, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My -- my specific question, sir, was whether the 1st Battalion commander ever reported at any point in time to you about information that he may have discovered concerning the events in Maline.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would like to say: When I received the task -- because this was the time when the brigade command had not assembled, until the 18th or the 19th. At no point in time was I able to do that. My battalion commanders were out in the field with the unit, so I was not able to call them to me and request information from them, because they were carrying out combat duty. Their main tasks were combat operations. They had their own organs, just like I had my own organs. The battalion commander, and I myself as the brigade battalion commander, we had our duties. So they were supposed to carry out a joint investigation and inform me about what they had found out. They were not able to do that because they were out in the field in combat with their soldiers. So he wasn't able to do that. But it was sufficient that his commander would inform -- his assistant would inform my assistant and that for me would be sufficient information as commander to find out what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, my final question: Were you ever made aware of any investigations by the 3rd Corps Command concerning the events in Maline or Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is 20 to 6.00. We are going to take the break and we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. I give the floor to the Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions arising from the questions put to you by my -- by my learned friend. On several occasions you had been asked why you informed your superior command about the presence of the Mujahedin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of a brigade and as a professional soldier, can you tell me whether an officer is duty-bound to inform his superior command about any fact that might have an impact on the performance of his mission, irrespective of the fact whether that fact has anything to do with the brigade or it is beyond the scope of the brigade's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am a responsible officer, and as such I believe that it was my duty and my obligation to inform my superior commander about the situation in my unit as well as anything that might have been going on in my immediate vicinity. It was my belief that the commander had to know all of that and that all that could help him to perform his duties and carry out his mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason, Mr. Sipic, why your reports contain information on the behaviour of the HVO, of the civilian protection, and other such things that you deemed were of significance and that your superior command should be aware of?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that something was mentioned in your report because you believed that this was of some significance for your superior command because it might have an impact on the combat readiness of your brigade and its mission, does that mean that the fact that you mentioned in your report was at the same time the fact for which your superior commander was responsible or did you include that particular fact only to keep your commander abreast of all the factors present in your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My commander had to be informed about all the factors existing in my area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, I want to clarify this situation -- when my learned friend asked you about your reporting and when you reported to the command of the 3rd Corps about the presence of the Mujahedin and other similar groups. My question to you is as follows: Did it mean to you that this command was responsible for them, or was that just one more factor that was present in your area?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not imply that my command was responsible for those groups. I just wanted to inform them of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also been asked several questions regarding foreigners and their presence in the area. You have clearly replied that these foreigners were not under your command and control but you were informed about their presence because they were a problem to you. My question to you is as follows: Since you were the commander of a brigade in the area where some of these foreigners were, tell me, please, did you ever personally or any of your subordinate commanders issue any orders to these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever as the brigade commander receive information that your superior command, either the West OG or the Bosanska Krajina OG or the 3rd Corps, at any time while you were a commander issue any orders to these Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such order ever having been issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, during the time when you were commander, did you ever receive a report from these Mujahedin about the way they performed some of their duties in the camp or in the general area?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did you know that the Mujahedin ever sent any reports to your superior command describing their behaviour, who they cooperated with, and so on and so forth? Did you ever receive any such information?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you something about the renegade soldiers, and you said that you could only look for the members of the 306th Brigade. The question that was put to you was if you ever went to Poljanice to see whether any of them were there. Tell me, were the laws of our country binding upon the commander? Did they make him look after his own soldiers and instigate measures against them should they leave their unit?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I had the authority only over my men, members of the brigade. And if they deserted, I had the obligation and duty under the law to institute measures against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that your military police went to the person's house to see if they were there. Was that one of the measures that meant the beginning of a procedure -- a procedure in order to establish where your soldier was, or was this just an exercise to gather information on his residence?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was to check where the soldier was. We did not make house-calls without a reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If your security organ or the military police established that this person had deserted, if they learnt of their whereabouts, would they continue investigating or would they stop at finding his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would continue investigating according to their possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, you have been shown a document in which you point to the problem of Arabs having money, buying weapons, and this was very early on in March 1993. Tell me, please: Were you aware as the commander, as a professional soldier, and as a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina that people were mobilised and that equipment was requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already explained to us, the BiH army did not have especially at the beginning any resources in order to provide soldiers with equipment and weapons. Were you familiar with the orders according to which the citizens were ordered to hand over all the equipment and arms that they had in their possession? Were you familiar with the order of the Secretariat that people were to be mobilised and that equipment would be requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was the Secretariat that was in charge of all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, at the moment when people were mobilised and equipment requisitioned, were people entitled to a free disposal with these things?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These things were to be used for a very specific purpose, the purpose for which they were requisitioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a person was mobilised and his rifle, hunting rifle, or some other type of weapon requisitioned, would it be the command of the brigade that would decide how the weapons would be used, which soldiers would take it to the front line, or was it up to the previous owner of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From then on, it was the brigade that had a say in how resources would be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, at the moment when a person decides to sell such a weapon, this meant that he acted against the property of the army.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly how we interpreted it and that's how we acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained how you were received when you attempted to enter the Mujahedin camp in Poljanice. Tell me, please: During your stay there, did you ever learn how many Mujahedin were stationed in that camp?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the brigade commander during that period, I never had precise information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have precise information as to how many Bosniaks whom you have mentioned in your documents, how many Bosnians had joined the Mujahedin in their camp in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have precise information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, while you were the commander of the 306th Brigade, for the reasons that you have already testified about - and I mean recruitment, recruiting people with money and humanitarian aid - could you assess what was the percentage of the local population that supported the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not engage in that research. There was a certain number; however, I didn't analyse it. I never came up with any percentages. I only knew that a certain number of people from the area supported them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned only a few of the elements. Would a responsible commander have to be aware of all the previously mentioned elements in order to be able to use force against such an armed group, irrespective of its size?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. Every operation that is to be undertaken has to have the so-called intelligence support, and this intelligence support consists of all the relevant information that would be used for the planning of such an operation. Secondly, I state once again that as a commander, I could not undertake any operation, military or other, before I received an order from my superior. I couldn't even undertake an operation against the HVO unless we were attacked. It was only under those circumstances that I could launch an operation, in order to protect my equipment and my men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know as commander that a commander at every level, if that was not an integral part of their mission, were they in the position to reach a decision without a prior order of the superior command?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of today's cross-examination, you were talking about the events and measures that you instigated in order to carry out investigation and learn what had happened with the kidnapped civilians and members of the HVO on the 8th of June, 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told my learned friend that after the investigation which was carried out, you received information from your assistant for security. And if I interpret your words well, you said that you didn't have any reason not to believe that this assistant had done whatever was necessary.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it customary in the military practice and doctrine that a commander, once he has issued an order to his subordinate, irrespective of the level of command, that he should believe that his subordinate will do everything that is within his jurisdiction and within his role? Is it normal for a commander to trust his superior?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the prerequisite of the chain of command. If there's no trust, there can be no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty as commander, I'm sure you received a number of orders from the corps commander in which it is stated that you, as the brigade commander, are responsible for the execution of the order. Did you receive such orders?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it's normal -- was it normal for a corps commander that if you inform him about the implementation of an order, that he would trust you or believe you as his brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The corps commander or any other officer by law or under military rules or under the circumstances in real life is not obliged to come out into the field and carry out the task that you're supposed to do and inform him that you are being -- you are in the process of implementing it successfully.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The superior command -- is this the situation that you can talk about? If you encounter a problem in the implementation of orders, would you then ask for help? And is it then the duty of the superior command commander to provide certain assistance, or does he have to come every day and involve himself in your implementation of the order?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by request or if it happens to be in his assessment to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to look at one of the orders which you also received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at DH65. That is a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the command of the 3rd Corps of the 19th of June, 1993. Is that the order that you have in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 19th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like -- we won't discuss the order itself but only item 6, which I just asked you about. Is it a customary part of an order when a commander orders his subordinate commander or unit for him to carry out the order, for him to be responsible for that order, and also to have the confidence in his commander that the order will be implemented? This item 6, is that the manner in which the superior officer conducts himself towards his subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the confidence and trust and your responsibility to implement orders, I would just like you again in this set of documents which I showed to you to look in this first part, document after number 10 or document under number 10. That is number 1903. Have you found it? It's the first set of documents, document number 1903. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already replied to my learned friend's question on the 12th - the 11th or the 12th - at a meeting of the inner command you received information from the security assistant that there was the killing of 20 arrested civilians and members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the last sentence of this information that you sent to the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Investigation is underway and once it is completed, you will be informed about the results in due time."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you sent the information out to the 3rd Corps and at the same time informed the 3rd Corps that the investigation was underway, was this a sign for your superior commander that his subordinate commander was doing what he was supposed to be doing?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any need now for some superior command to come to your area where you and your organs were conducting an investigation in order to conduct a parallel investigation?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is something that was not supposed to happen and did not happen in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So by implementing the order that you need to adhere strictly to the law, you were actually implementing your mission in the usual way it is done in any army.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Sipic, in view of the fact that you established once the investigation was completed that these Mujahedin had committed this act, can you please tell me whether the problem created by somebody who was not a member of the army obliges you as a commander to carry out other measures other than the ones that you already did undertake.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will have some questions for Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipic, during the cross-examination, you were shown a number of documents. I don't think that there is any need for you to read them again, since you've already analysed them. These are documents of the Prosecution, 679, 660, 661, 662, 663. So I would like to ask you to clarify just these following things: In these documents, when the 7th Muslim Brigade is mentioned, the 314th Brigade, the Mujahedin, would you agree with me that in the course of your testimony you differentiated clearly between the Mujahedin and the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when you were writing these reports or your subordinates were doing so or assistant commander, when the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin were mentioned that in these reports the Mujahedin were not represented as members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony today in response to my learned friend's questions, you were shown a document, Prosecution Exhibit P704, and that is an order about the resubordination of a part of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the village of Kljaci and you have explained how this came about. What I would like to ask you is as follows, and you already said that, that these members of the 7th Muslim Brigade at that point were resting in the Bila Valley in the Kljaci village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Sipic, that soldiers of the 7th Brigade or your own brigade, at the point in time when they were resting, were they there without weapons? They had gone to their homes without weapons, which they had left in their home units?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time when this order was issued, the one that you signed, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were practically without weapons.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, were you able to provide them with weapons in the event of combat or possible conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to do that for my own members, and I could not definitely do it for members of the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: One more question I would like to clarify with you: You mentioned several times the renegade soldiers, members of either the 7th Muslim Brigade or the 314th Brigade. Would you agree with me that when you say "a renegade member of the 7th Muslim" or any other brigade, that this meant that that soldier or those soldiers were no longer members of the B and H army or members of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly why they are described as "renegade soldiers." At one point in time, they were members of those units but then they were out of control [as interpreted] and they happened to be in these certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the commander of the battalion or the brigade did not have control over those soldiers and were not able to issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that there is a mistake in the transcript, line 10 and 11. Not that they were out of control but once they had left the unit, they were no longer under the control of the battalion or the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document DH269, and that will relate to some questions put by my learned friend during the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were today presented by a document -- exhibit of the Prosecution, P663, presenting some problems relating to the status of the Mujahedin and - I repeat - and members of the 7th Muslim Brigade which were stationed in that area. I asked you yesterday and you confirmed: According to what you know the 7th Muslim Brigade was not stationed in Mehurici and did not have any organised unit there is. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document, an official document of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. It's a letter sent to the Bosanska Krajina OG. And if possible, I would like you to read this very brief text.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the OG Bosanska Krajina, your request number 01/700-2 of the 5th of July, 1993. "We are not able to comply because on several occasions we had informed you officially that these units in the area -- in that area do not belong to the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade and we have no right to command and control those units at the Mehurici camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document confirm what we were just talking about, that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not stationed in Mehurici and that those soldiers or whatever they were there -- who were there, foreigners and local Bosnians, were not members of the 7th Muslim Brigade or members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have a few questions to put to you. I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one is relative to your arrival in the camp in Poljanice where you met a foreigner who told you that he had contacts with Halilovic. Who was Mr. Halilovic? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that to be Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the function or position of Mr. Sefer Halilovic in the army?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, the -- where was his office? Where was the office of the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then conclude that the Mujahedin in question went to Sarajevo to discuss things with the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I -- that's something that I don't know. I provided this information based on what they stated about those talks. I don't know whether they went or whether they didn't go. That is why I sent the information to the command of the 3rd Corps, so that they could check if that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At your level he told you that he had met with the highest ranking officer in the army. Did you believe -- believe him, or maybe he was lying to you and telling you stories. What did you think?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible at that moment in time, because his goal was for me to leave that camp in Poljanice as soon as possible. I received this information, but I was not able to check it. I could have doubted it or not doubted it, and I could have written it down or not. However, I did pass it on for the superiors up there who had the right contacts with the General Staff to check whether it was really possible that this was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have also told us about the problems that you had with the HVO and the HOS, and you have even told us that they were more extreme, the latter were more extreme. Can you tell the Chamber who these people were? Who were the members of the HOS?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were members -- the members were of -- were both from the Croat and the Bosniak population, who were in the HOS. Then in the HVO there were some more extremist forces, commanded by Jandric, who was feared by all the people in the Travnik valley, in Central Bosnia. Still to this day he is a threat to that whole area because he's involved in crime, kidnappings, blackmail, threats. On one occasion his group met me when I was going from Mosor to Travnik on that road and it was terrible for me. They all were wearing bull horns on their heads, about 20 of them. A gang ran out from the woods. They stopped my vehicle and my driver. And I didn't have any security. It was just myself and the driver. I didn't know what to do at that moment, and luckily -- luckily they let me go. They forced me -- they gave me one bottle of plum brandy and forced me to drink it. They asked me, "Where are you going?" I told them that I was going to a meeting with the HVO regarding the resolution of certain problems, and they said, "Well, go but pay attention to how you will resolve them." So that was one personal experience that I had with those forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people who belonged to the HOS, did they have a geographic area that they controlled and were they facing your forces or were they people who just arrived in the area without any control or organisation?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while HOS was together with the HVO. They coordinated their actions, but they were characteristic because they wore black uniforms, they had insignia -- "U" insignia on their caps. They were black. They wore black, including gloves in order to look as terrifying as possible. You could see them in Travnik, in Vitez. They had tasks of their own that nobody else was aware of. I know that afterwards they became a part or joined the composition of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Another question: In your -- in the 306th Brigade, how many men did you have under you, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 1.960 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were responsible for 1.960 men, almost 2.000, during your tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During your command, how many people were killed and how many were injured?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the total that the brigade had, the number of persons who were killed. But according to the stages, I don't know the exact data. I know that at the end of the war, that brigade, according to some indications, had about 136 casualties, those who were killed, and there were also from three to four hundred wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take the document number 663 and go back to the page where there is the following sentence -- just a moment. This is a Prosecution exhibit. Have you got the document 663? This is a document that you signed but you didn't draft it. The date is 5 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it. It's a mistake. This is not the 5th of May document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was addressed to the West OG in Bugojno, and the date is 5 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the last page, there is a proposal. Actually, there are six proposals. Can you please look at the fifth proposal. Can you please read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To resolve the status of the Mujahedin and members of the 17th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us that you obtained a degree in political sciences, so you can appreciate the meaning of a sentence. When you read this sentence, the word "status," "To resolve the status of the Mujahedin," does the word "status" also apply to the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here what is meant is the status of the Mujahedin and the status of the 7th. There's a mistake here. It's not the 17th, because there was never a 17th Muslim Brigade. So what is meant is the renegade groups, the 7th Muslim Brigade, to resolve their status because they had left the 7th but remained in that area. So this was to see whether the superior command would decide where they would be mobilised or for the 7th to give us lists of who these people were so that we could resolve their status so that we would stop them from walking around without any control, without knowing why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that this sentence has two aspects: The status of the Mujahedin has to be resolved, and also the question of some of the groups of the 7th Brigade has to be resolved. And this is way we have to understand this proposal.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may return the document to the usher. My last question, very brief question: The Defence has given you document, DH -- which is relative to the investigation of the event in Maline and in which it says that the superior command will be advised of the results of the investigation in due course. When you say that this event in Maline was the result of the action of the Mujahedin, and when you learned that, did you report to the 3rd Corps saying that after the end of the investigation hereby we inform you that the action was carried out by the Mujahedin and that members of the BiH army were not involved? Did you send a report saying that -- what the results of the investigation were? As far as I can remember. It was almost ten years ago, and it might be difficult for you to answer this question. However, you have been shown a document in which you informed your superior command that you would advise them of the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I ordered my security assistant, Asim Delalic, who was conducting the investigation, to inform in writing about the results of the investigation and to send that to the superior command. He informed me that he had sent this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he show you this report or not?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, because I was out in the field with the units. I was in touch with him, and I didn't doubt. If I had ordered it and that -- and he reported back to me, there was no reason for me to doubt that he did actually implement my order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at your level, you knew that he had sent a report to the 3rd Corps with the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theoretically speaking, this report should be found in the archives of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the archives of the 306th Brigade, it should be there as well, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be there at the security organ, because it's their report. So it should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I'm going to ask the two parties whether they have any questions arising from the Judges' questions. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any time in May of 1993 were you informed by any source that Sefer Halilovic actually went to the camp in Poljanice and met with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in response to a question from the Presiding Judge in terms of casualties, you said you were only aware of the number of casualties within the 306th Mountain Brigade at the end of the war or by the end of the war. And I just wanted to be clear about that. Were you referring to the casualties from the commencement of the war through approximately December 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
